opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest with yourself about what you can't do. If you're a small lab, you're not going to win by training the biggest model. The big companies have tens or hundreds of thousands of GPUs, huge data pipelines, and large engineering teams. If you try to compete on that axis, you'll just be a smaller, slower version of them, and that's not a good position.

So the question becomes: where is the leverage? I'd point to three things.

First, **ideas that change the scaling curve, not just move along it.** Big labs are optimized to push the existing recipe further: more data, more compute, more RL. That works, but it leaves a lot of fundamental questions underexplored. How does the model actually learn representations? Why does a certain training dynamic lead to reasoning, or to collapse? If you understand the mechanism, you can sometimes get a 10x or 100x efficiency gain, and that's something compute alone doesn't give you. A small lab can afford to think deeply about one problem for a long time, which a product-driven org often can't.

Second, **pick problems where insight matters more than scale.** For example, efficient inference, long-context memory, better ways of doing search and planning on top of a model, or understanding why certain post-training methods work. You can often study these with small models and controlled experiments, and the findings transfer. A lot of my own work has been like that: you build a simplified setting, you analyze it mathematically, and then you check whether the prediction holds in larger systems. That loop is cheap and very informative.

Third, **talent density and speed.** A new lab has no legacy. No internal politics, no ten teams that need to agree. If you have a small group of people who are really strong and really motivated, you can iterate much faster than a big company. But it only works if everyone is genuinely excited about the research direction, not just there for the brand or the salary.

I'd also add a caution: don't chase whatever is hot this month. By the time a direction is obviously hot, the big labs already have fifty people on it. A small lab needs a bit of contrarian conviction, betting on something that looks unfashionable now but that you believe, for principled reasons, will matter in two or three years.

And finally, you need a way to stay grounded. Pure theory with no connection to real systems can drift. So I'd say: keep one foot in understanding, one foot in building something that actually works, even at small scale. If you can show that your idea makes a real system better or cheaper, people will pay attention, regardless of how many GPUs you have.

r001.rationale: The response identifies fast iteration as a key advantage for a small lab and says controlled experiments can make the research loop cheap and informative.

r002.rationale: It says a small lab cannot win by training the biggest model and argues for ideas that change the scaling curve instead of merely pushing the existing recipe further.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes understanding mechanisms such as how models learn representations and why training dynamics work, presenting that deeper understanding as a source of efficiency beyond compute alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing a new lab has to accept is that it cannot win by playing the same game as the big companies. If you try to train the biggest model with the most data, you will lose, because that game is decided by compute and capital, not by ideas. So the question becomes: where does a small team actually have an advantage?

I'd say three places. The first is speed and focus. A big company has many internal customers and many political constraints, and a lot of research gets shaped by what the product teams need this quarter. A small lab can pick one or two hard questions and just stay on them for a year without anyone asking for a roadmap. That kind of concentration is rare and it's genuinely valuable.

The second is picking problems where the bottleneck is understanding rather than scale. There is still a lot we do not understand about why these models work: how reasoning emerges, what the training dynamics are actually doing, why certain architectures generalize and others do not. Those questions can be studied on small models, sometimes on toy models, and the insights transfer. If you find something real at small scale, the big labs will often verify it at large scale for you, and that is fine. You get credit for the idea, and the field moves forward.

The third is efficiency itself as a research direction. If you have one tenth or one hundredth of the compute, then making training and inference cheaper is not a side project, it is survival. That constraint forces you to be creative, and historically a lot of the most important algorithmic ideas came from people who simply could not afford to be wasteful.

On the practical side, I'd keep the team small and very senior at the beginning. Hire people who can go end to end, from the math to the systems code, because you cannot afford layers of specialization yet. Stay open. Publish, release code, talk to the community, because for a small lab reputation compounds faster than anything else, and it is how you attract the next good person and the next collaborator with GPUs.

And be honest with yourself about the timeline. You should expect that the first year produces mostly understanding and infrastructure, not headline results. If the founders have the patience for that, I actually think this is a very good moment for small labs, because the frontier of ideas has not been exhausted at all. Only the frontier of scale is expensive.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes speed and focus, plus making training and inference cheaper. It does not identify improving the efficiency of research iteration as a central challenge.

r002.rationale: It says a small lab cannot win by training the biggest model with the most data and that the frontier of scale is expensive, conveying that scale alone may be insufficient.

r003.rationale: It identifies understanding why models work as a bottleneck and says those questions can be studied at small scale, with insights that transfer.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what can a small team learn that a big company is not already set up to learn? If you simply follow the same roadmap with less compute and fewer people, it’s very difficult to compete.

So I would start with a focused research question where you can run experiments quickly. You have some hypothesis about why current methods are inefficient or where they fail, and you design the smallest experiment that can tell you whether that hypothesis is right. You don’t need to train the largest model to get a useful answer to every question.

A small lab also has an advantage in how quickly it can change direction. The researchers can discuss an idea, implement it, and look at the results without coordinating across many teams. But you have to use that flexibility deliberately. If you spread five people across ten unrelated directions, you lose it.

The goal, initially, should be to produce a clear insight and convincing evidence. Then you can decide whether it deserves more resources. I would be ambitious about the question, but very disciplined about the cost of answering it.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes running quick, small experiments and using limited resources efficiently, making faster research iteration a central strategy for the small lab.

r002.rationale: It advises against simply following the same roadmap with fewer resources, but does not state that scaling laws alone may be insufficient.

r003.rationale: It recommends forming hypotheses about where methods fail and seeking clear insights, but does not connect deeper problem understanding to success beyond scaling laws.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to choose your questions carefully. If you’re a new lab, you probably don’t want to start by doing exactly what a large company is doing, just with less compute. You need a direction where a small team can learn something important without having to operate at that scale.

For example, you can start with a smaller, controlled setting where you can run experiments quickly and understand why something works. Then you ask: does this insight carry over as we scale up? A small experiment doesn’t automatically tell you what will happen in a large model, so that connection has to be tested.

There’s also a balance between having a long-term research question and getting feedback quickly. You want a clear hypothesis, an experiment that could prove it wrong, and a short enough cycle that you can change direction. For a new lab, that ability to move quickly and build a deeper understanding can be a real advantage.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes short feedback cycles, quick experiments, and the ability to change direction quickly as an advantage for a new lab.

r002.rationale: It says results from small experiments must be tested before extrapolating to larger models, but does not state that relying on scaling laws alone may be insufficient.

r003.rationale: It values understanding why something works and building deeper understanding, but does not connect that need to going beyond what scaling laws provide.
